html:
In the 19th century India went from the world's largest exporter of cotton cloth to an importer of it. Historians call this the de-industrialisation of India.

About 1750 India made perhaps a quarter of the world's manufactured goods, above all hand-woven cottons (see Indian calicoes). Britain kept them out of its home market with bans and high duties while its own cotton mills grew up behind that wall.

In 1813 Parliament ended the East India Company's monopoly of trade with India. Machine-spun yarn and cloth from Lancashire came in at a duty of a few per cent. They were cheap, and prices fell further each decade. Indian exports of fine cloth had almost stopped by the 1830s. Dhaka, home of the famous muslin, shrank from about 150,000 people to perhaps a third of that. Spinning by hand, which had given millions of women some income, nearly vanished. Weavers of coarse cloth held on, using British yarn.

India's share of world manufacturing fell to about 2 per cent by 1900. How much was due to British policy and how much to the machine itself is still argued.

Naoroji and later nationalists made it a main charge against British rule, and Gandhi made the spinning wheel their symbol. Indian-owned mills began in Bombay in 1854.
sum: In the 19th century India went from the world's largest exporter of cotton cloth to an importer of it. Historians call this the de-industrialisation of India.
